sampling_model.design: Independent regime samples with fixed reference law \(\mu_0\) and known compact supports.
sampling_model.units: For every \(p\in\mathcal A\), observe \(Y_{p,1},\ldots,Y_{p,n_p}\stackrel{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}P_p\), independently across regimes.
sampling_model.treatment: The regime label indexes an interventional law or a conditionally identified law; the common-rank equation fixes the same-unit coupling.
sampling_model.overlap: No treatment-propensity overlap is needed after the regime laws are identified; density nondegeneracy is \(b\le f_p\le B\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Project each regime density at \(k_n\), use the strictly positive fallback off the computable regularity event, solve the normalized Monge--Ampere problem, smooth the potential at \(h_n\), form \(\widetilde H_p\), and clip spectrally at \(m/4\) before every inverse and margin statistic. Clipping is provably inactive on any raw-Hessian event satisfying \(r_{H,n}\le m/2\). Establishing that this event has class-uniform probability at least \(1-\delta\) requires the unresolved boundary-wavelet, extension-kernel, response-remainder, influence-envelope, increment, and Bernstein-net estimates; it is not a model assumption.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Section 5.3 states that there is no precise characterization of structural causal models inducing cyclically monotone counterfactuals.

Section 3.1, Definition 1 and equation (6), together with Theorem 2, show that invertible cyclically comonotone production functions make \(h_1\circ h_0^{-1}\) the Brenier natural-trend map and identify the treated counterfactual distribution by its pushforward.

NeurIPS Theorem 4.12, repeated as Appendix Theorem B.11 in equations (13) and (72), claims strict Euclidean monotonicity for time-one dynamic optimal-transport counterfactual maps under a uniform-cube Markovian source and Lemma 4.6/B.5 regularity.
Theorem 2.1 represents conditional vector quantiles as gradients of convex functions from a common absolutely continuous reference law.
The paper proves pointwise central limit theorems for smooth plug-in Brenier maps on a flat torus and rules out global weak convergence in high dimension.
Theorems 1 and 2 establish near-matching minimax integrated squared-error rates for smooth optimal-transport map estimation.
Theorems 1.3 and 1.5 give global potential stability and characterize the conormal linear response along smooth density paths.

body.tldr: Separate Brenier structure does not guarantee that a same-unit counterfactual composition preserves Euclidean ranks. The exact population frontiers and the robust counterexample to the published Euclidean implication are unconditional, as is the fixed-support Le Cam lower separation rate. The reported Hessians remain everywhere defined by clipping at \(m/4\); on the explicitly observed raw-Hessian event with \(r_{H,n}\le m/2\), clipping is inactive and the rank-margin interval and separated test decisions are deterministically valid. A class-uniform probability bound for that event, and therefore the upper separation rate \((\log n/n)^{s/(2s+d)}\), remain conditional on the unresolved endpoint-response, wavelet, kernel, influence, and concentration program. The eventual validated chord certificate retains its stronger source-product trigger and is deterministic once the required band event and small-radius conditions hold.

project_justification.gap: Torous, Gunsilius, and Rigollet (2024), Section 3.1, Definition 1 and Theorem 2, identify a nonlinear difference-in-differences counterfactual law under cyclical comonotonicity, but do not give the symmetric-cross-Hessian Euclidean frontier, the Hessian-commutation cyclic-gradient frontier, the global margin, or inference for it. Ribeiro, Santhirasekaram, and Glocker's displayed dynamic-transport assumptions admit the audited open-neighborhood Brenier counterexample even though its symmetric cross-Hessian is indefinite. Existing statistical optimal-transport results provide integrated map risk or pointwise map limits, not a bounded-domain class-uniform raw-Hessian band. In particular, the cited response and elliptic papers do not supply the order-zero Hessian modulus, quadratic remainder, or estimator concentration chain needed for such a band.
project_justification.niche: The delivered field-tier contribution is a graph-native common-rank Brenier counterfactual frontier: exact Euclidean and cyclic structural characterizations, an observable rank margin, a robust published-claim counterexample, an unconditional lower testing frontier, and a deterministic event-to-margin certificate. The class-uniform upper band and matching upper rate are a clearly isolated conditional program rather than an asserted consequence of lower-derivative stability.
project_justification.fill: The symmetric cross-Hessian theorem characterizes Euclidean monotonicity, the commutation theorem characterizes the cyclic-gradient subfamily, and the open-neighborhood matrices separate the full common-rank Brenier class from the stronger commuting subclass and refute the audited Euclidean implication under the displayed dynamic assumptions. The estimator uses a positive density fallback and \(m/4\) spectral clipping on every sample. The event-to-band theorem proves that, whenever \(\max_p\lVert\widetilde H_p-H_p\rVert_\infty\le r_{H,n}\le m/2\), clipping is inactive and all margin and threshold conclusions follow. A separate conditional corollary lists the exact endpoint, wavelet, kernel, response, influence-kernel, and Bernstein-net estimates that would yield probability at least \(1-\delta\) and the selected upper rate. The fixed-support quadratic-bump mixture continues to prove the lower rate unconditionally, and the validated certificate continues to use its distinct stronger source-product trigger.

body.related_work: De Lara and Ganassali (2025), Section 5.3, leave the cyclically monotone SCM characterization unresolved. Torous, Gunsilius, and Rigollet (2024), Section 3.1, Definition 1 and equation (6), define cyclical comonotonicity and show that it makes the relevant inverse composition cyclically monotone; their Theorem 2 uses that condition to identify a treated counterfactual law in nonlinear difference-in-differences. Their framework does not supply the pointwise symmetric-cross-Hessian Euclidean frontier, the Hessian-commutation cyclic-gradient frontier, the sharp global margin, or margin inference, and the common-rank Brenier framework does not claim their difference-in-differences identification result. Ribeiro, Santhirasekaram, and Glocker (NeurIPS 2025), Theorem 4.12 and Appendix Theorem B.11, assert strict Euclidean monotonicity under their displayed dynamic-transport conditions, but their proof uses a state-dependent weighted inner product; the audited open-neighborhood Brenier pair satisfies those displayed conditions while its Euclidean symmetric cross-Hessian is indefinite. Carlier, Chernozhukov, and Galichon (2016), Theorem 2.1, provide common-reference vector quantiles, not inverse-composition geometry. Hutter and Rigollet (2021) establish integrated map-risk rates. Manole et al. (2024) provide plug-in and boundary-wavelet machinery, and Manole et al. (2023) provide pointwise torus map limits, but neither source proves this bounded-domain simultaneous raw-Hessian band. Caja-Lopez, Delgadino, and Kitagawa (2026), Theorem 1.3, control \(C^{1,\alpha}\) potential error, while Theorem 1.5 gives a \(C^{2,\beta}\)-valued differentiable path and its conormal response; neither gives the class-uniform order-zero Hessian modulus or quantitative quadratic remainder used by the conditional program. Dong, Lee, and Kim (2020), Theorem 1.7, gives \(C^1\) regularity for a divergence-form conormal problem, whereas Theorem 1.10 concerns a different nondivergence oblique problem; neither furnishes the missing Hessian estimate. Ghosal and Sen (2022) study rank maps rather than cross-Hessian margins, and Chen and Fang (2019) motivate caution for ordinary bootstrap claims at degenerate nonsmooth functionals. None of these sources provides the validated source-product interval search, whose sufficient trigger remains distinct from the scalar margin endpoint except in the proved small-radius comparison.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The raw Hessian response is order zero and may accumulate a logarithm, while signed high-order smoothing need not preserve positive definiteness. Spectral clipping at \(m/4\) therefore totalizes the statistic. The proved theorem makes clipping inactive only on the explicitly defined event \(\mathcal B_n\) when \(r_{H,n}\le m/2\); it does not prove that event's probability. The conditional probability program still needs a uniform boundary-wavelet projection, a bounded polynomial-reproducing extension kernel, the endpoint linearization and quadratic remainder, influence-kernel variance and envelope bounds, an increment bound, and matrix-Bernstein/net concentration. The finite certificate additionally uses a source-product allowance \((2M+r_{H,n})r_{H,n}t_{\mathrm{ch}}^2\lVert z\rVert_2^2\), and its trigger is not equivalent to the scalar margin trigger at arbitrary radii. Validated interval arithmetic remains necessary, and the lower bound retains its strict-slack nondegeneracy qualification.
body.honest_scope: The exact Euclidean and cyclic structural frontiers, the NeurIPS-assumption-aligned open-neighborhood witness, the deterministic event-to-margin theorem, the explicit fixed-support Le Cam lower family, and the small-radius validated-certificate implication are proved components. The boundary-uniform Hessian endpoint modulus, the quantitative quadratic remainder, and the wavelet/kernel/influence concentration chain are open; none is supplied by the cited sources. Accordingly, class-uniform coverage, the upper separation rate, and a matching two-sided testing frontier are conditional on the explicitly listed analytic and stochastic program, whereas the lower separation rate is unconditional. The certificate's source-product trigger is a distinct stronger sufficient condition, with no arbitrary-radius equivalence to the scalar negative-margin endpoint and no termination claim at zero margin. No adaptation, irregular-support, coordinate-invariance, unvalidated-numerics, or empirical-violation claim is made. The scalar and simultaneously diagonal cases still reduce to positive derivative ratios.
